narration_use: reference only when drafting; required units must be derivable from the public B2 inputs (table + intent)
file_naming: one G1 per input contract; B1/B3/B4/B5 need separate drafts
intent: To demonstrate that the United States tax system is largely flat rather than progressive when all tax types are combined, challenging the common perception that the wealthy pay a significantly higher share of their income.

units.meaning: Combined tax burden across income groups is only modestly varying and not strongly progressive; it does not rise steadily with income.
units.computation: sum of value across all listed tax-type rows for each entity
accepted_routes: Combined taxes stay in a moderate band, roughly 23.7% to 31.5% of income, rather than climbing steeply with income.
The overall tax burden does not rise steadily from poorest to richest; it is relatively flat with only modest variation.
When all tax types are combined, the pattern is not a strong progressive rise.
units.visual_evidence_rule: The total combined tax burden for each income group must be visually comparable across the distribution, at least for Poorest, 5th, 10th, and Richest.
units.temporal_anchor: the narration clause saying the tax system as a whole is not very progressive / is mostly flat
units.reviewer_question: Should the video be required to convey the overall flat/moderate combined-burden pattern, or is that interpretation optional?

units.meaning: The Richest income group's total tax burden is lower than the Poorest group's and lower than the 10th group's; it is the lowest total burden among the listed groups.
units.computation: Richest total - Poorest total = 23.700 - 24.104 = -0.404 percentage points; Richest total - 10th total = 23.700 - 31.507 = -7.807 percentage points
accepted_routes: Richest pays 23.7% of income in total taxes, below Poorest at 24.1% and far below the 10th group at 31.5%.
The richest group is the lowest total-tax group, not the highest.
The billionaire at the top pays a smaller overall share than everyone else, including the poorest.
units.visual_evidence_rule: The total-tax values for Richest, Poorest, and 10th must be visually comparable so the Richest-lower-than-Poorest and Richest-lower-than-10th relationships can be read.
units.temporal_anchor: the narration clause about the billionaire paying a smaller portion than everyone else, even the poorest
units.reviewer_question: Must the video make the Richest-below-Poorest comparison explicit, or only show overall flatness?

units.meaning: Income taxes alone are progressive across most of the distribution, rising sharply from lower to higher income before the Richest group falls below the 10th group.
accepted_routes: Income taxes rise from 1.003% for the 2nd group to 17.998% for the 10th group, then fall to 10.003% for the Richest.
Income taxes look strongly progressive up through the 10th group, but the Richest is lower than the 10th.
The progressive impression comes mainly from income taxes alone, not from all taxes combined.
units.visual_evidence_rule: The income-tax component must be visible or separable enough to show the rise from lower/middle groups to the 10th group and the drop at Richest.
units.temporal_anchor: the narration clause saying that if you look at certain types of taxes, it is natural to assume rich people pay a bigger burden
units.reviewer_question: Should income-tax progressivity be included as required context for the contrast, or is it optional background?

units.meaning: The tax mix differs by income: lower-income groups rely mostly on consumption and payroll taxes, while the Richest group relies more on corporate/property and income taxes.

basis.note: Poorest-Consumption taxes share of Poorest tax mix
Poorest-Payroll taxes share of Poorest tax mix
Richest-Corporate and property taxes share of Richest tax mix
Richest-Income taxes share of Richest tax mix
Richest-Consumption taxes share of Richest tax mix
Richest-Payroll taxes share of Richest tax mix

accepted_routes: For the Poorest, consumption and payroll taxes are about 51.9% and 44.0% of the tax mix; for the Richest, corporate/property and income taxes are about 44.3% and 42.2%.
Lower-income groups pay mostly through consumption and payroll taxes, while the Richest pays mostly through corporate/property and income taxes.
The composition of taxes shifts from payroll/consumption at the bottom to income/corporate-property at the top.
units.visual_evidence_rule: The tax-type composition for at least Poorest and Richest must be visible so their different shares of the tax mix can be compared.
units.temporal_anchor: the narration clause about putting these taxes together and seeing a big change
units.reviewer_question: Must the video show tax-mix composition differences, or is only the combined total required?

units.meaning: The combined payroll-plus-consumption tax burden as a share of income is far larger for lower-income groups than for the Richest group.
units.computation: for each entity, payroll taxes value + consumption taxes value; Poorest = 10.602 + 12.499 = 23.101; 5th = 10.399 + 7.0 = 17.399; Richest = 0.397 + 1.999 = 2.396
accepted_routes: The Poorest group pays 23.1% of income in payroll plus consumption taxes, compared with 2.4% for the Richest.
Payroll and consumption taxes are a much larger income share at the bottom than at the top.
Regressive payroll/consumption taxes are far heavier for the Poorest and 5th group than for the Richest.
units.visual_evidence_rule: Payroll and consumption tax values for Poorest, 5th, and Richest must be available or combinable so the large lower-income versus Richest contrast can be seen.
units.temporal_anchor: the narration clause about poor people paying about the same portion as rich people when taxes are combined
units.reviewer_question: Should the regressive payroll/consumption component be explicitly conveyed, or is it optional mechanism?

optional_valid: Payroll taxes are a large but relatively stable percentage of income for most lower/middle groups, e.g. 10.602% for Poorest and 10.399% for 5th, before dropping to 0.397% for Richest.
Estate taxes appear only for the 10th group (0.303% of income) and Richest (0.801% of income) in the table.
Consumption tax burden falls from 12.499% for Poorest to 1.999% for Richest.
unsupported_to_avoid: Causal explanations for why the tax system is flat, such as loopholes or policy capture.
Dollar amounts paid rather than shares of income.
Claims that every income group pays exactly the same combined tax rate.
Claims that the Richest pays less in every single tax type, especially income tax or corporate/property tax.
Any statement that the Poorest pays 0% income tax; the table has no Poorest income-tax row.
Extrapolating beyond the listed income groups or into future trends.
Chart/layout prescriptions such as bar/line type, colors, axis ticks, or positions.
notes: All value-based totals are sums of the table's value column across listed tax-type rows for that entity; relative_value is used only for tax-mix composition. Missing rows, such as Poorest income tax, are not treated as zero unless explicitly stated.
weight_mode_note: every unit gets 1/n so coverage is a plain share; weight_template is kept for per-type analysis only
